claims.source: It can be divided into at least four subgroups: (1) relapse-remitting MS (over 80% patients), (2) secondary progressive MS (the late phase of relapse-remitting type), (3) primary progressive MS (about 10% patients), and (4) relapse-progressing MS (about 5% patients), all of which are characterized by chronic inflammation in the CNS (Steinman, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature on MS classification.

claims.claim: MS inflammatory lesions consist of various immune cells, including CD4+ T cells and MHC class II+CD11b+ monocytes/macrophages.
claims.source: MS inflammatory lesions consist of various immune cells, including CD4+ T cells and MHC class II+CD11b+ monocytes/macrophages, and subsequent loss of neurological function in the CNS due to the disruption of neural circuits that regulate various organ functions (Steinman, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature on MS pathology.

claims.claim: Several complications including mental illnesses and gastrointestinal failures are associated with MS.
claims.source: Indeed, several complications including mental illnesses and gastrointestinal failures are associated with MS (Goldman Consensus Group, 2005; Gupta et al., 2005; Kimura et al., 2000; Marrie et al., 2015; Pokorny et al., 2007; Rang et al., 1982; Sadovnick et al., 1989).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to literature documenting MS complications.

claims.claim: EAE development is dependent on autoreactive helper T cells (pathogenic CD4+ T cells), particularly Th1 and Th17 cells.
claims.source: EAE development is dependent on autoreactive helper T cells (pathogenic CD4+ T cells), particularly Th1 and Th17 cells and many immune cells are accumulated at the affected sites such as CD8+ T cells, macrophages, B cells, and neutrophils. (Arima et al., 2012, 2015; Jäger et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on EAE pathogenesis.

claims.claim: The transfer EAE model is completely dependent on MOG-specific CD4+ T cells (pathogenic CD4+ T cells) including Th17 and Th1 populations, while it is not dependent on CD8+ T cells.
claims.source: Therefore, the transfer EAE model is completely dependent on MOG-specific CD4+ T cells (pathogenic CD4+ T cells) including Th17 and Th1 populations, while it is not dependent on CD8+ T cells because of no CD8+ T cells in the transferred pathogenic T cell population.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the experimental design where only CD4+ T cells are transferred, logically excluding CD8+ T cell dependence.

claims.claim: There are many papers that describe the involvement of not only IL-17A but also IFN-γ particularly from pathogenic CD4+ T cells including activated Th1 and Th17 cells for the development of EAE models.
claims.source: Importantly, there are many papers that describe the involvement of not only IL-17A but also IFN-γ particularly from pathogenic CD4+ T cells including activated Th1 and Th17 cells for the development of EAE models including the transfer EAE ones (Duhen et al., 2013; El-behi et al., 2010; Goverman, 2009; Jäger et al., 2009; Ottum et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to literature on cytokine involvement in EAE.

claims.claim: Stress conditions can cause gastrointestinal diseases via the brain-gut axis.
claims.source: Stress conditions can cause gastrointestinal diseases via the brain-gut axis.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field of brain-gut interactions.

claims.claim: The brain-gut axis involves interactions between neural components, including the autonomic nervous system, the central nervous system, the stress system such as the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, and the corticotropin-releasing factor system, and intestinal factors.
claims.source: Animal models have shown that this axis involves interactions between neural components, including the autonomic nervous system, the central nervous system, the stress system such as the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, and the corticotropin-releasing factor system, and intestinal factors such as the intestinal barrier, the luminal microbiota, and the intestinal immune response (Allen et al., 2014; Bonaz and Bernstein, 2013; Caso et al., 2008; Stengel and Taché, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on brain-gut axis mechanisms.

claims.claim: Details about the underlying molecular mechanisms, including the relationship between each of these components, are lacking.
claims.source: However, details about the underlying molecular mechanisms, including the relationship between each of these components, are lacking.
claims.evidence: This claim represents a knowledge gap identified by the authors based on literature review.

claims.claim: Brain micro-inflammation at blood vessels specific in the boundary area of the third ventricle region, thalamus, and dentate gyrus is established by pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under stress conditions.
claims.source: We demonstrate that brain micro-inflammation at blood vessels specific in the boundary area of the third ventricle region, thalamus, and dentate gyrus is established by pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under stress conditions and induces fatal gastrointestinal failure via a paraventricular nucleus (PVN)/dorsomedial nucleus of the hypothalamus (DMH)-vagal pathway.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing immune cell accumulation at specific brain vessels under stress conditions.

claims.claim: The gateway reflex triggered by stress-mediated PVN activation induced the accumulation of immune cells at specific vessels in a manner dependent on CCL5.
claims.source: Mechanistic analysis suggested that the gateway reflex triggered by stress-mediated PVN activation induced the accumulation of immune cells, including pathogenic CD4+ T cells and MHC class IIhiCD11b+ cells, at these specific vessels in a manner dependent on CCL5.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing CCL5 expression at specific vessels and the effect of CCL5 blockade on immune cell accumulation.

claims.claim: The resulting brain micro-inflammation enhanced a new neural pathway including neurons in the PVN and DMH, and vagal nerve-mediated gastrointestinal failure via micro-inflammation-dependent ATP.
claims.source: The resulting brain micro-inflammation enhanced a new neural pathway including neurons in the PVN and DMH, and vagal nerve-mediated gastrointestinal failure via micro-inflammation-dependent ATP.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing ATP production, neural activation, and the effects of ATP receptor blockade.

claims.claim: Blockade of the regional brain micro-inflammation and establishment of the new neural pathway inhibited the gastrointestinal pathology.
claims.source: Accordingly, blockade of the regional brain micro-inflammation and establishment of the new neural pathway inhibited the gastrointestinal pathology.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing therapeutic effects of various interventions.

claims.claim: Pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under the stress condition caused a severe phenotype including sudden death.
claims.source: Pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under the stress condition of the current study caused a severe phenotype including sudden death (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by clinical score and mortality data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Either stress or pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer alone did not cause the severe phenotype.
claims.source: On the other hand, either stress or pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer alone, or stress with the transfer of activated CD4+ T cells specific for irrelevant antigens such as ovalbumin or a retinal autoantigen, interphotoreceptor retinoid-binding protein (IRBP), did not cause the severe phenotype, although the retina-specific activated CD4+ T cells accumulated in the eyes (Figure 1A and B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing different treatment groups shown in figures.

claims.claim: Blood aldosterone and cortisol levels were significantly higher in mice with stress even without pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer.
claims.source: Blood aldosterone and cortisol levels were significantly higher in mice with stress even without pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B), suggesting stress-mediated activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by hormone measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B.

claims.claim: Chronic stress conditions cause a severe and atypical phenotype of EAE, which might represent progressive MS.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that chronic stress conditions cause a severe and atypical phenotype of EAE, which might represent progressive MS.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data and comparison to MS clinical presentations.

claims.claim: Mice induced with pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under stress excreted bloody stools.
claims.source: We noticed that mice induced with pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under stress, but not either treatment only, excreted bloody stools (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fecal occult blood test data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Blood hematocrit levels decreased in mice with pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under stress.
claims.source: Consistently, blood hematocrit levels decreased (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by hematocrit measurement data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The blood content came from the stomach and upper level of the intestine.
claims.source: We found the blood content came from the stomach and upper level of the intestine (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by tissue analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Focal bleeding lesions in the stomach were detected by histopathological analysis.
claims.source: Focal bleeding lesions in the stomach were detected by histopathological analysis (Figure 2D, black spots), and tissue distraction including epithelial necrosis was evident particularly in the stomach and upper level of the intestine (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological data shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claims.claim: Under very strong stress, the activation of p38 and MAPKAPK2 contributes to stomach epithelial destruction under muscarinic M3 receptor signaling via acetyocholine derived from vagus nerve.
claims.source: It has been reported that under very strong stress, the activation of p38 and MAPKAPK2 contributes to stomach epithelial destruction under muscarinic M3 receptor signaling via acetyocholine derived from vagus nerve (Debas and Carvajal, 1994; Jia et al., 2007; Uwada et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on stress-induced gastric pathology.

claims.claim: Phosphorylated p38 and phosphorylated MAPKAPK2 were detected in the gastric mucosa of mice with pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under stress condition.
claims.source: We investigated the activation status of p38 and MAPKAPK2 in stomach isolated from mice with pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under our stress condition and detected phosphorylated p38 and phosphorylated MAPKAPK2 in the gastric mucosa (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Treatment with a proton pump inhibitor, lansoprazol, suppressed the severe phenotype in mice with pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under stress condition.
claims.source: Consistent with dysregulation of gastrointestinal region, the treatment with a proton pump inhibitor, lansoprazol, suppressed the severe phenotype in mice with pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under stress condition (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing therapeutic effects of lansoprazol shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Increase of plasma potassium levels was observed in mice with pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under stress condition.
claims.source: Furthermore, increase of plasma potassium levels, most likely following the gastrointestinal bleeding, was observed in mice with pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under stress condition (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by plasma potassium measurement data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: Heart failure was detected in mice with pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under stress condition by a cardiac electrocardiogram system.
claims.source: Heart failure was detected in mice with pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under stress condition by a cardiac electrocardiogram system (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting a heart failure at least partially mediated by high potassium ions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ECG data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Donor pathogenic CD4+ T cells and MHC class II+ cells first accumulate at the L5 cord within 5 days after pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer via the gravity-gateway reflex.
claims.source: Donor pathogenic CD4+ T cells and MHC class II+ cells first accumulate at the L5 cord within 5 days after pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer via the gravity-gateway reflex as described previously (Arima et al., 2012; Sabharwal et al., 2014) (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3A and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Chronic stress caused pathogenic CD4+ T cells and MHC class II+ cells to accumulate at specific vessels of the boundary region of the third ventricle region, thalamus, and dentate gyrus, but not in the L5 cord.
claims.source: In the present work, chronic stress caused pathogenic CD4+ T cells and MHC class II+ cells to accumulate at specific vessels of the boundary region of the third ventricle region, thalamus, and dentate gyrus, but not in the L5 cord (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The L5 cord vessels are no longer used as a gateway for immune cells toward the CNS under chronic stress conditions.
claims.source: These data suggested that the L5 cord vessels are no longer used as a gateway for immune cells toward the CNS under chronic stress conditions.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that immune cells do not accumulate at L5 under stress conditions.

claims.claim: Pathogenic CD4+ T cells and MHC class II+ cells accumulated comparably at the brain specific vessels regardless of lansoprazol treatment in mice with pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under stress condition.
claims.source: We also found that pathogenic CD4+ T cells and MHC class II+ cells accumulated comparably at the brain specific vessels redardless of lansoprazol treatment, which suppressed gastrointestine dysregulation (see Fiugre 2F), in mice with pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under stress condition (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: MHC class IIhiCD11b+ cells originated from the peripheral organs rather than resident microglia cells.
claims.source: Td-tomato labeling of microglia cells, which we used previously (Arima et al., 2015), revealed that MHC class IIhiCD11b+ cells originated from the peripheral organs rather than resident microglia cells (Figure 3D), suggesting that the MHC class IIhiCD11b+ cells that accumulated at the specific vessels were activated monocytes from the peripheral organs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Various immune cells, including CD8+ T cells, B cells, NK cells, and neutrophils, had accumulated at the specific vessels.
claims.source: Moreover, we found that various immune cells, including CD8+ T cells, B cells, NK cells, and neutrophils, had also accumulated at the specific vessels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Blockade of CCL5 significantly suppressed the accumulation of pathogenic CD4+ T cells and MHC class IIhiCD11b+ cells at the specific vessels.
claims.source: Blockade of CCL5, but not chemokines including CCL2, CX3CL1, significantly suppressed the accumulation of pathogenic CD4+ T cells and MHC class IIhiCD11b+ cells at the specific vessels (Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and reduced clinical scores and mortality (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing effects of CCL5 neutralization shown in Figures 4A, B, and C.

claims.claim: The stress condition even without pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer induced CCL5 expression at the specific blood vessels.
claims.source: Interestingly, the stress condition even without pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer induced CCL5 expression at the specific blood vessels, but acute stress models did not. (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data showing CCL5 mRNA expression shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Neutralization of IFN-γ or IL-17A inhibited the brain micro-inflammation at the specific vessels.
claims.source: Moreover, neutralization of the Th1 cytokine, interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), or that of the Th17 cytokine, IL-17A, also inhibited the brain micro-inflammation at the specific vessels (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing effects of cytokine neutralization shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The accumulation of IL-17A- or IFN-γ-deficient pathogenic CD4+ T cells was significantly reduced at the specific blood vessels under stress conditions.
claims.source: Importantly, the accumulation of IL-17A- or IFN-γ-deficient pathogenic CD4+ T cells was significantly reduced at the specific blood vessels under stress conditions and resulted in less mortality (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using cytokine-deficient T cells shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Both IFN-γ and IL-17A from pathogenic CD4+ T cells are necessary for the accumulation at specific vessels and the severe phenotypes.
claims.source: These data suggested that both IFN-γ and IL-17A from pathogenic CD4+ T cells are necessary for the accumulation at specific vessels and the severe phenotypes.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing effects of cytokine deficiency and neutralization.

claims.claim: Brain micro-inflammation induced by microinjection of pathogenic CD4+ T cells plus MOG-pulsed DC or inflammatory cytokines at specific vessels developed severe gastrointestinal failure and affected mortality.
claims.source: We found that brain micro-inflammation induced by these treatments developed severe gastrointestinal failure and affected mortality (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing effects of direct cytokine injection shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Anti-CCL5 antibody treatment had no significant effect on mortality of mice with microinjections of cytokines at the specific vessels under stress condition.
claims.source: Furthermore, we investigated the mortality of mice with microinjections of cytokines at the specific vessels under stress condition in the presence or absence of anti-CCL5 antibody treatment and found anti-CCL5 antibody treatment had no significant effect (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: CCL5 mainly contributes to the accumulation of immune cells including pathogenic CD4+ T cells at the specific vessels, while the effect of cytokine injection is CCL5-independent.
claims.source: This result suggested that CCL5 mainly contributes to the accumulation of immune cells including pathogenic CD4+ T cells at the specific vessels, while the effect of cytokine injection is CCL5-independent.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that CCL5 blockade does not affect cytokine-induced pathology.

claims.claim: Microinjection of 6-OHDA at the specific vessels successfully depleted TH+ sympathetic neurons and phospho-CREB signals.
claims.source: Microinjection of 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) at the specific vessels successfully depleted tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)+ sympathetic neurons and phospho-CREB signals that were induced by noradrenergic receptor signaling after sympathetic activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: 6-OHDA-mediated chemical sympathectomy suppressed immune cell accumulation at the specific vessels and the development of fatal gastrointestinal failure.
claims.source: 6-OHDA-mediated chemical sympathectomy suppressed immune cell accumulation at the specific vessels and the development of fatal gastrointestinal failure in mice that received pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under stress condition (Figure 5A–5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing effects of sympathectomy shown in Figures 5A and 5B.

claims.claim: PVN neurons include TH+ neurons that are activated by several stresses, especially chronic ones.
claims.source: It is reported that PVN neurons include TH+ neurons are activated by several stresses, especially chronic ones (Herman and Cullinan, 1997; Ramot et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2013; Ulrich-Lai and Herman, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on PVN neuron activation.

claims.claim: PVN TH+ neurons were specifically activated by stress condition even without EAE induction.
claims.source: Consistent with these results, we found that PVN TH+ neurons were specifically activated by stress condition even without EAE induction (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The activation of PVN neurons, particularly THneg neurons, was enhanced in mice with pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under stress condition.
claims.source: Moreover, the activation of PVN neurons, particularly THneg neurons, was enhanced in mice with pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under stress condition (Figure 5C), suggesting the crosstalk between microinflammation at the specifc vessels and PVN.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Injection of a retrograde neural tracer, cholera toxin B (CTB), at specific vessels reached the PVN.
claims.source: We found that injection of a retrograde neural tracer, cholera toxin B (CTB), at specific vessels of the boundary area of third ventricle region, thalamus, and dentate gyrus reached the PVN (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neural tracing data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: TH+ neurons at the PVN co-expressed noradrenaline transporter, but not dopamine transporter.
claims.source: In addition, TH+ neurons at the PVN co-expressed noradrenaline transporter, but not dopamine transporter (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting that they secrete noradrenaline at the specific vessels, which we have shown to be important for chemokine induction (Arima et al., 2012, 2015; Sabharwal et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: An anterograde tracer, PHA-L, injected at specific vessels mainly reached the DMH and to a lesser degree the PVN.
claims.source: We found that an anterograde tracer, PHA-L, injected at these vessels mainly reached the DMH and to a lesser degree the PVN (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neural tracing data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: CTB injection at the DMH region reached the specific vessels.
claims.source: Consistent with this result, CTB injection at the DMH region reached the specific vessels (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neural tracing data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: DMH neurons, particularly THneg ones, were highly activated after pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under stress condition.
claims.source: Importantly, DMH neurons, particularly THneg ones, were highly activated after pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under stress condition (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The injection of pathogenic CD4+ T cells plus MOG-pulsed DC or IL-17A plus IFN-γ cytokines at the specific vessels under stress condition enhanced neural activation of the PVN and DMH.
claims.source: Consistent with this notion, the injection of pathogenic CD4+ T cells plus MOG-pulsed DC or IL-17A plus IFN-γ cytokines at the specific vessels under stress condition enhanced neural activation of the PVN and DMH (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: The ablation of PVN and DMH sites significantly inhibited brain micro-inflammation, gastrointestinal disease and mortality.
claims.source: Furthermore, the ablation of PVN and DMH sites significantly inhibited brain micro-inflammation, gastrointestinal disease and mortality (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing effects of neural ablation shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: The activation of DMH neurons is suppressed by GABA-A receptor activation.
claims.source: It is reported that the activation of DMH neurons is suppressed by GABA-A receptor activation (Rusyniak et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on DMH neuron regulation.

claims.claim: Muscimol injection at DMH suppressed gastrointestinal disease and mortality.
claims.source: Muscimol, GABA-A receptor agonist, injection at DMH suppressed gastrointestinal disease and mortality (Figure 5I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing effects of muscimol treatment shown in Figure 5I.

claims.claim: DMH activation following the microinflammation at the specific vessels is critical for the development of fatal gastrointestinal disease.
claims.source: All these results suggested that DMH activation following the microinflammation at the specific vessels is critical for the development of fatal gastrointestinal disease.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from multiple experimental results showing the role of DMH in pathology.

claims.claim: ATP is a neurotransmitter and is expressed in several cells after cytokine stimulation.
claims.source: ATP is a neurotransmitter and is expressed in several cells after cytokine stimulation (Burnstock, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on ATP function.

claims.claim: The expression of ATP was enhanced after IL-17A plus IL-6 stimulation in endothelial cells in vitro.
claims.source: We found that the expression of ATP was enhanced after IL-17A plus IL-6 stimulation in endothelial cells in vitro (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Neurons in the DMH were highly activated by the microinjection of ATP at the specific vessels under stress condition.
claims.source: Neurons in the DMH were highly activated by the microinjection of ATP at the specific vessels under stress condition (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: Blockade of the ATP receptor, P2RX7, at the specific vessels by A438079 suppressed the neural activation and fatal gastrointestinal failure.
claims.source: Moreover, blockade of the ATP receptor, P2RX7, at the specific vessels by A438079, a selective antagonist, suppressed the neural activation and fatal gastrointestinal failure (Figure 6B and C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing effects of P2RX7 blockade shown in Figures 6B and C.

claims.claim: Neurons around the specific vessels expressed P2RX7.
claims.source: Neurons (Neurofilament L-positive cells) around the specific vessels expressed P2RX7 and after cytokine or ATP stimulation, neurons in the DMH region also showed NFATc1 activation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), which is a downstream signaling component of P2RX7 (Grol et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: NFATc1 is a downstream signaling component of P2RX7.
claims.source: Neurons (Neurofilament L-positive cells) around the specific vessels expressed P2RX7 and after cytokine or ATP stimulation, neurons in the DMH region also showed NFATc1 activation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), which is a downstream signaling component of P2RX7 (Grol et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on P2RX7 signaling.

claims.claim: ATP can be sensed by neurons that connect specific vessels to the DMH region in a manner dependent on P2RX7 expression.
claims.source: Thus, we suggested that ATP can be sensed by neurons that connect specific vessels to the DMH region in a manner dependent on P2RX7 expression.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing P2RX7 expression and ATP effects.

claims.claim: The status of PVN neurons affects the homeostasis of gastrointestinal organs via branches of the vagal nerves.
claims.source: We next investigated whether vagal nerve activation is involved in the development of the severe gastrointestinal failure triggered by brain micro-inflammation, because (i) the status of PVN neurons affects the homeostasis of gastrointestinal organs via branches of the vagal nerves (Ferguson et al., 1988) and (ii) the DMH is connected to the vagal neurons at the dorsal motor vagal nucleus (DMX), where the nucleus of the vagal nerves are present (Thompson et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on PVN-vagal connections.

claims.claim: The DMH is connected to the vagal neurons at the dorsal motor vagal nucleus (DMX).
claims.source: We next investigated whether vagal nerve activation is involved in the development of the severe gastrointestinal failure triggered by brain micro-inflammation, because (i) the status of PVN neurons affects the homeostasis of gastrointestinal organs via branches of the vagal nerves (Ferguson et al., 1988) and (ii) the DMH is connected to the vagal neurons at the dorsal motor vagal nucleus (DMX), where the nucleus of the vagal nerves are present (Thompson et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on DMH-DMX connections.

claims.claim: PHA-L after injection at the DMH reached the DMX.
claims.source: PHA-L after injection at the DMH reached the DMX as described (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by neural tracing data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The DMX is highly activated after the injection of pathogenic CD4+ T cells with MOG-pulsed DC at the vessels under stress condition.
claims.source: Moreover, we found that the DMX is highly activated after the injection of pathogenic CD4+ T cells with MOG-pulsed DC at the vessels of the boundary area of the third ventricle region, thalamus, and dentate gyrus under stress condition (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Nucleus of the Tractus Solitaries (NTS) was activated after injection of pathogenic CD4+ T cells with MOG-pulsed DC at the vessels under stress condition.
claims.source: In addition, we found that Nucleus of the Tractus Solitaries (NTS), which is the main nucleus of afferent vagus nerves, was activated (Figure 7A), suggesting that afferent neuronal activation is induced by severe gastrointestinal failure, most likely in a manner dependent on micro-inflammation-related ATP in gastrointestinal regions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Vagotomy suppressed gastrointestinal failure and mortality in EAE mice under stress.
claims.source: Finally, we found that vagotomy suppressed gastrointestinal failure and mortality in EAE mice under stress (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing effects of vagotomy shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Severe gastrointestinal failure is induced by enhanced neural activation via the DMH-vagal axis, which is activated by brain micro-inflammation at the specific vessels under stress.
claims.source: These results suggest that severe gastrointestinal failure is induced by enhanced neural activation via the DMH-vagal axis, which is activated by brain micro-inflammation at the specific vessels under stress.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from multiple experimental results showing the neural pathway involved in pathology.

claims.claim: Brain micro-inflammation at the boundary area of the third ventricle region, thalamus, and dentate gyrus develops severe gastrointestinal failure via the DMH-vagal pathway in a transfer EAE model under stress.
claims.source: We here showed that brain micro-inflammation at the boundary area of the third ventricle region, thalamus, and dentate gyrus develops severe gastrointestinal failure via the DMH-vagal pathway in a transfer EAE model under stress.
claims.evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings supported by multiple experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: Pathogenic CD4+ T cells transverse toward the central nervous system (CNS) through a gateway at the dorsal vessels of the fifth lumbar (L5) spinal cord in steady state in response to gravity-mediated chemokine expression via regional sympathetic activation, a phenomenon called the gravity-gateway reflex.
claims.source: We have reported that pathogenic CD4+ T cells transverse toward the central nervous system (CNS) through a gateway at the dorsal vessels of the fifth lumbar (L5) spinal cord in steady state in response to gravity-mediated chemokine expression via regional sympathetic activation, a phenomenon we call the gravity-gateway reflex (Arima et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: Artificial electric stimulations in different muscles establishes the immune cell gateways at different regions of the dorsal vessels of spinal cord, a phenomenon called the electric-gateway reflex.
claims.source: During the gravity-gateway reflex, we found that artificial electric stimulations in different muscles, which mimic specific sensory-sympathetic crosstalk, establsihes the immune cell gateways at different regions of the dorsal vessels of spinal cord, a phenomenon we call the electric-gateway reflex (Arima et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: Pain induces sympathetic-mediated alterations in ventral vessels of the spinal cord to establish gateways to cause EAE relapse, a phenomenon called the pain-gateway reflex.
claims.source: We also found that pain induces sympathetic-mediated alterations in ventral vessels of the spinal cord to establish gateways to cause EAE relapse, a phenomenon we call the pain-gateway reflex (Arima et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: Under stress condition, a gateway forms at the vessels of boundary area of third ventricle region, thalamus, and dentate gyrus, which is described as the stress-gateway reflex.

results.result: Chronic stress combined with pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer causes a severe EAE phenotype with high mortality, while either stress or T cell transfer alone does not produce this severe outcome. This severe phenotype may represent progressive MS.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C20, C21 demonstrate clear experimental evidence showing that the combination of chronic stress and pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer is necessary and sufficient for the severe phenotype with high mortality. Control experiments with stress alone, T cells alone, or irrelevant antigen-specific T cells show no severe phenotype. However, C23's speculation about representing progressive MS is an inference without direct validation.

results.result: Pathogenic CD4+ T cell transfer under stress induces fatal gastrointestinal failure characterized by bloody stools, decreased hematocrit, focal bleeding lesions in the stomach and upper intestine, activation of p38/MAPKAPK2 signaling, elevated plasma potassium, and heart failure.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27, C29, C31-C32 provide convergent evidence from multiple methodologies (fecal occult blood tests, hematocrit measurements, histopathology, Western blots, ECG) demonstrating severe gastrointestinal pathology. C30 shows therapeutic intervention with lansoprazol suppresses the phenotype, supporting the gastrointestinal mechanism. The causal chain from GI bleeding to hyperkalemia to heart failure (C32) is reasonably inferred but involves some speculation.

results.result: Under chronic stress conditions, pathogenic CD4+ T cells accumulate at specific brain vessels (boundary area of third ventricle, thalamus, dentate gyrus) rather than at the L5 spinal cord, establishing brain micro-inflammation via a stress-gateway reflex.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35 demonstrate a clear shift in immune cell accumulation from L5 cord (without stress) to specific brain vessels (with stress), supported by immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry data. C2, C16, and C80 describe this phenomenon as the stress-gateway reflex. The anatomical specificity is well-documented, though the mechanistic details of why stress redirects accumulation require further investigation.

results.result: CCL5 expression at specific brain vessels, induced by chronic stress, is required for recruitment of pathogenic CD4+ T cells (particularly Th1 and Th17 cells) to establish brain micro-inflammation. Both IFN-γ and IL-17A from pathogenic CD4+ T cells are necessary for accumulation and severe phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 show CCL5 blockade significantly reduces immune cell accumulation and mortality, with CCL5 expression induced by chronic (but not acute) stress. C41-C43 demonstrate that both IFN-γ and IL-17A are required, using neutralizing antibodies and cytokine-deficient T cells. The data converge to support a CCL5-dependent recruitment mechanism requiring both Th1 and Th17 cytokines.

results.result: Direct microinjection of pathogenic CD4+ T cells plus antigen-presenting cells or inflammatory cytokines (IFN-γ, IL-17A, IL-6) at specific brain vessels is sufficient to induce fatal gastrointestinal failure under stress, independent of CCL5.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C44 demonstrate sufficiency through direct injection experiments showing gastrointestinal failure and mortality. C45-C46 show that CCL5 blockade does not affect cytokine-induced pathology, distinguishing the recruitment phase (CCL5-dependent) from the effector phase (CCL5-independent). This establishes that brain micro-inflammation itself, once established, is sufficient to drive pathology.

results.result: The PVN-sympathetic pathway is involved in establishing brain micro-inflammation at specific vessels. Stress activates PVN TH+ neurons that project to specific brain vessels, and chemical sympathectomy suppresses immune cell accumulation and gastrointestinal failure.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48 show that 6-OHDA-mediated sympathectomy depletes TH+ neurons and suppresses both immune cell accumulation and gastrointestinal failure. C50-C53 demonstrate PVN TH+ neuron activation by stress and neural connections to specific vessels via retrograde tracing. The convergent evidence from lesion studies, neural tracing, and immunohistochemistry strongly supports PVN involvement in the gateway reflex.

results.result: Brain micro-inflammation activates a neural pathway involving DMH neurons, which is critical for fatal gastrointestinal failure. Ablation or pharmacological inhibition of DMH suppresses gastrointestinal disease and mortality.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 establish bidirectional neural connections between specific vessels and DMH using anterograde and retrograde tracers, with enhanced DMH activation after pathogenic T cell transfer under stress. C57-C58 show that cytokine injection activates DMH and that DMH ablation inhibits pathology. C60 demonstrates muscimol (GABA-A agonist) suppresses disease, confirming DMH's critical role through multiple complementary approaches.

results.result: ATP, produced by endothelial cells after cytokine stimulation, acts as a neurotransmitter that activates DMH neurons via P2RX7 receptors, serving as a molecular switch for the neural pathway mediating gastrointestinal failure.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65 demonstrate that IL-17A plus IL-6 stimulation induces ATP production in vitro, ATP injection activates DMH neurons, and P2RX7 blockade suppresses neural activation and gastrointestinal failure. C66 shows P2RX7 expression on neurons around specific vessels. The convergent evidence from in vitro studies, pharmacological blockade, and immunohistochemistry supports ATP as a critical mediator, though the in vivo ATP measurements at specific vessels would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: The DMH-vagal nerve pathway mediates fatal gastrointestinal failure. DMH projects to dorsal motor nucleus of vagus (DMX), which is activated by brain micro-inflammation, and vagotomy suppresses gastrointestinal failure and mortality.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 demonstrate DMH-DMX connectivity via anterograde tracing and DMX activation after cytokine injection. C73 shows NTS (afferent vagal nucleus) activation, suggesting bidirectional vagal involvement. C74 provides the critical functional evidence that vagotomy suppresses gastrointestinal failure and mortality. The convergent evidence from neural tracing, activation markers, and surgical intervention strongly supports the DMH-vagal pathway as the effector mechanism.

results.result: While stress activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (elevated aldosterone and cortisol), this axis has minimal role in micro-inflammation-mediated gastrointestinal disease, as corticosteroid receptor antagonists do not suppress the pathology.
results.evaluation: Claim C22 demonstrates HPA axis activation through elevated hormone levels. C103 shows that corticosteroid receptor antagonists (mifepristone and guggulsterone) do not suppress gastrointestinal disease after cytokine injection. C104 infers minimal HPA involvement based on this negative result. The evidence supports that while HPA is activated, it is not the primary mediator of the gastrointestinal pathology in this model.

results.result: MHC class IIhiCD11b+ cells that accumulate at specific brain vessels originate from peripheral organs (activated monocytes) rather than resident microglia, and various other immune cells (CD8+ T cells, B cells, NK cells, neutrophils) also accumulate at these sites.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 uses Td-tomato lineage tracing to definitively show peripheral origin of MHC class IIhiCD11b+ cells. C38 documents accumulation of multiple immune cell types via flow cytometry. C36 shows that lansoprazol treatment (which suppresses GI pathology) does not affect immune cell accumulation, dissociating the recruitment phase from the effector phase. The lineage tracing provides strong evidence for peripheral origin.

results.result: Stress reduces mouse movement and soleus muscle stimulation, leading to decreased L5 DRG activation and chemokine expression at L5 dorsal vessels, potentially explaining closure of the L5 gateway under stress.
results.evaluation: Claim C81 reports behavioral observations, and C82 shows reduced L5 DRG activation and chemokine expression under stress. However, C83 is explicitly speculative about the causal mechanism. While the correlation between reduced movement and reduced L5 gateway activity is documented, the causal link and the specific role of soleus muscle stimulation require direct experimental validation (e.g., forced soleus stimulation under stress conditions).

results.result: MHC class IIhiCD11b+ cells isolated from stressed EAE mice can activate pathogenic CD4+ T cells without exogenous MOG peptide, suggesting autoantigen-presentation ability.
results.evaluation: Claim C96 is supported by in vitro co-culture experiments showing IL-2 production (T cell activation marker) when naïve MOG-specific T cells are cultured with CD11b+ cells without adding MOG peptide. This demonstrates functional antigen presentation capability, though the identity of the presented antigen and whether it is truly MOG-derived requires further characterization.

results.result: Background on MS pathogenesis, EAE models, and brain-gut axis: MS is a CD4+ T cell-mediated CNS autoimmune disease with multiple subtypes and complications including gastrointestinal failures. EAE models depend on pathogenic CD4+ T cells (Th1/Th17). The brain-gut axis involves multiple neural and immune components, but molecular mechanisms are incompletely understood.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C15 provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These claims accurately represent the current understanding of MS, EAE models, and brain-gut interactions. C15 identifies a knowledge gap that motivates the current study. These are well-established facts in the field rather than novel findings.

results.result: Previous work by the authors established gateway reflexes: gravity-gateway reflex (L5 dorsal vessels), electric-gateway reflex (muscle stimulation-dependent), and pain-gateway reflex (L5 ventral vessels for EAE relapse).
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79 accurately cite the authors' previous published work on gateway reflexes. These are established findings from prior studies that provide context for the current stress-gateway reflex discovery. The citations are appropriate and the descriptions match the published literature.

results.result: Background on pain-gateway reflex and resident monocytes: CX3CL1 is critical for EAE relapse after pain in recovered mice. CNS-resident activated monocytes persist long-term and express CX3CL1 after norepinephrine stimulation, suggesting a CX3CR1-CX3CL1 autocrine loop.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C93 describe previous findings from the authors' work and related literature on tissue-resident immune cells. C91 and C93 involve some speculation about patrolling monocytes as the origin and the autocrine loop mechanism, but these are reasonable inferences from the data. This provides important context distinguishing the current stress-gateway reflex (CCL5-dependent, no resident monocytes) from the pain-gateway reflex (CX3CL1-dependent, resident monocytes present).

results.result: The recruitment of MHC class IIhiCD11b+ cells may be partially dependent on CX3CL1 from endothelial cells, induced by cytokines from pathogenic CD4+ T cells that accumulated via CCL5.
results.evaluation: Claim C95 is explicitly speculative ("we assume") and proposes a mechanism for monocyte recruitment downstream of initial T cell accumulation. While this is a reasonable hypothesis based on the authors' previous work, it lacks direct experimental validation in the current study. Testing this would require CX3CL1 blockade experiments or CX3CR1-deficient monocyte transfer studies.

results.result: Cytokines from pathogenic CD4+ T cells (IFN-γ, IL-17A, IL-6) act on endothelial cells to induce ATP production, which then activates the DMH-vagal pathway leading to p38/MAPKAPK2 activation in gastric mucosa and epithelial destruction.
results.evaluation: Claims C28, C105-C106 cite literature establishing that stress-induced vagal activation causes gastric pathology via p38/MAPKAPK2. C107 demonstrates cytokine-induced ATP production in vitro. C108 infers the in vivo mechanism connecting these observations. The logic is sound and supported by the combination of in vitro data and literature, though direct measurement of ATP at specific vessels in vivo would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: Clinical relevance: MS patients show concurrence with inflammatory bowel diseases, and primary progressive MS is dominant in patients with bowel dysfunction, suggesting the transfer EAE under stress model may represent progressive MS.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C110 cite clinical literature documenting MS-GI comorbidities. However, C111's suggestion that the model represents progressive MS is speculative. While there are phenotypic similarities (chronic stress, severe pathology, GI involvement), the model lacks key features of progressive MS (e.g., gradual neurological decline, demyelination patterns) and no direct validation against human progressive MS pathology is provided.

results.result: Speculation on broader implications: Brain micro-inflammation occurs in various neurodegenerative diseases and may activate neural pathways to cause organ dysfunction. MHC class II genetic associations support potential involvement of autoreactive CD4+ T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C115 cite literature on neuroinflammation in various diseases and genetic associations. However, C116 and C125 are explicitly speculative extrapolations from the current findings to broader disease mechanisms. While the hypothesis is interesting and supported by genetic associations, it requires direct experimental validation in models of these other diseases.

results.result: Speculation on stress sensitivity and clinical prediction: Individual stress sensitivity may be determined by autoreactive CD4+ T cell populations, potentially influenced by early life stress affecting T cell repertoire. Measuring autoreactive T cells in blood might predict susceptibility to stress-induced organ failure.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C122 cite literature on stress sensitivity, early life stress effects, and T cell development. However, C123-C124 are explicitly speculative proposals for clinical applications. While the hypothesis is logical given the experimental findings, it requires validation through: (1) measuring autoreactive T cell populations in stressed vs. non-stressed individuals, (2) correlating these with stress-induced pathology, and (3) prospective studies testing predictive value.

results.result: Speculation on therapeutic and mechanistic implications: Chemokine/cytokine expression and immune cell accumulation at specific vessels could be diagnostic/therapeutic targets. Brain micro-inflammation at specific vessels may activate neural pathways regulating various organ homeostasis, with potential bidirectional brain-periphery interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C97, C102, and C126 are explicitly speculative proposals for clinical applications and broader mechanistic principles. While these are reasonable extrapolations from the findings, they require validation through: (1) imaging studies detecting micro-inflammation in patients, (2) therapeutic trials targeting these pathways, and (3) experimental demonstration of periphery-to-brain signaling affecting micro-inflammation location.

results.result: Summary of proposed mechanism: Brain micro-inflammation at specific vessels (boundary of third ventricle, thalamus, dentate gyrus) develops via stress-mediated PVN activation and establishes a novel DMH-vagal neural pathway that causes fatal gastrointestinal failure. ATP acts as a switch activating this pathway.
results.evaluation: These claims synthesize the major findings into a coherent mechanistic model. C76, C98-C99, and C127 are well-supported by the convergent experimental evidence from neural tracing, lesion studies, pharmacological interventions, and functional outcomes. C101 cites relevant literature on cerebrovascular innervation. The proposed mechanism integrates multiple lines of evidence into a testable model, though some details (e.g., precise ATP signaling mechanisms) require further investigation.
